expectations.text: States that the MODEL ENDPOINT must move inside the tenant (e.g. Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI) — Bedrock cannot serve the data-bearing calls
expectations.evidence: 'Has to move (touches customer content)' table, first row: 'Bedrock inference | Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI'. The mental model is stated as 'Anything that touches customer content runs in their Azure subscription.' Note: the answer hedges on whether Bedrock could stay if it were in the client's own AWS account ('spend one email probing whether Bedrock in their own AWS account with PrivateLink + CMK ... is acceptable — it usually isn't'), but under the assumed reading (#2) it clearly places inference inside the Azure subscription.

expectations.text: States that the TRACE / OBSERVABILITY store must also move inside the boundary because traces contain client data
expectations.evidence: 'The fights you'll have' → '**Traces.** Datadog LLM Observability / Langfuse / whatever you're using captures prompt and completion bodies. That is a straight-line exfil path out of their tenant ... Either self-host the trace backend in their subscription, or redact payloads at the SDK boundary and ship only spans + metrics.' The 'traces contain client data' rationale is explicit.

expectations.text: States that LOG and AUDIT destinations must also live inside the tenant (not shipped to a vendor-owned aggregation account)
expectations.evidence: Move table: 'Bedrock model invocation logging | Foundry diagnostic settings → their Log Analytics / Blob | This log *contains prompts and completions*. It's customer data.' And in the bottom line: 'any log that carries a payload' moves. Only content-free aggregate telemetry is allowed to stay, with an explicit DPA carve-out required.

expectations.text: Explicitly warns that a SaaS observability vendor (e.g. hosted Langfuse/Datadog) breaks the residency clause
expectations.evidence: 'Datadog LLM Observability / Langfuse / whatever you're using captures prompt and completion bodies. That is a straight-line exfil path out of their tenant and their security team will find it.' Vendors named explicitly.

expectations.text: Identifies what CAN stay outside: things containing no client data (e.g. CI/CD, container registry/images, IaC, source code, dev/synthetic environments)
expectations.evidence: 'Can stay on AWS (no customer content)' section: 'Source code, prompt templates, model config, Helm charts, Terraform modules'; 'CI/CD (GitHub Actions or whatever) — it builds and deploys into their tenant, it doesn't process their data'; 'Container registry — but mirror images into their ACR'; 'Aggregate, content-free telemetry'. Also correctly flags Terraform state as needing an audit first, and that eval golden sets built from customer documents ARE customer data.

expectations.text: Notes that a cloud-agnostic Kubernetes core is what makes the move feasible and that only provider bindings change
expectations.evidence: 'Everything else stays portable *if it's already on Kubernetes*. Your EKS workloads move to AKS with real but bounded pain: IRSA → AKS Workload Identity (both are OIDC federation, the shape is the same), IAM roles → Entra managed identities + RBAC, SGs/NACLs → NSGs + NetworkPolicy'. The provider-binding seams are named explicitly ('Cut abstraction seams at exactly three places and keep one codebase: model provider, object store, vector/search store'), with the counter-case called out: 'If anything is on Lambda/Step Functions/DynamoDB Streams, that part is a rewrite, not a port.'

expectations.text: Distinguishes the compliance boundary as 'everything client data touches' rather than only the app and database
expectations.evidence: 'The clean mental model is BYOC / in-tenant data plane. Anything that touches customer content runs in their Azure subscription.' Operationalized as: 'Inventory every place a prompt, completion, or document body is written to disk or crosses a network boundary. That list *is* your migration scope — everything else is noise.' The move table extends well past app+DB (queues, parsing workers, invocation logs, guardrails, embeddings).

claims.claim: ~90% of enterprises mean the subscription/tenant boundary reading, and Azure OpenAI / AI Foundry satisfies it
claims.evidence: The 90% figure is fabricated precision — no source, and unverifiable. The underlying structural point (three readings of 'won't leave our tenant') is sound, but the statistic is invented.

claims.claim: The embedding model change forces a full corpus reindex and retrieval re-tuning, and this is bigger than the infra port
claims.evidence: 'The hidden cost nobody scopes' — a genuinely non-obvious and correct observation (embedding-space change invalidates chunking/reranker/top-k tuning). Notably this is a RAG-specific insight the with_skill run did NOT surface. It assumes the platform is a RAG system, which the prompt does not state, but it is flagged as a conditional cost, not a fact about the user's system.

claims.claim: Anthropic models are available in Microsoft Foundry
claims.evidence: Correctly hedged in-line: 'verify current model + region availability yourself, don't take my word for it. If Claude isn't available in their region, it's GPT-family or self-hosted.' The uncertainty is surfaced rather than asserted.

claims.claim: Bedrock in the client's own AWS account with PrivateLink + CMK could satisfy the clause and is worth probing
claims.evidence: Correct premise-challenge, same substance as the with_skill run's §5, though given one sentence rather than a structured decision point.

uncertainties: Model/region availability in Foundry is explicitly flagged as unverified and delegated to the reader

suggestions.reason: The baseline passed 7/7 — identical to with_skill. This eval has NO discriminating power as written. A strong base model already knows the residency split. Assertions must move to the layer the baseline actually misses.

Concrete gaps the baseline has that no assertion catches: (a) no mention that Azure audit surfaces are OFF BY DEFAULT (Foundry diagnostic settings, AKS control-plane logs) or that Foundry public network access is ON by default; (b) no log immutability / WORM (Object Lock equivalent) for audit evidence — it mentions Blob immutability only for the document store; (c) no Global-vs-Regional deployment residency trap; (d) no default-deny NetworkPolicy / zero-internet-egress target inside the tenant (it says 'Azure Firewall with an FQDN allowlist', which is weaker); (e) no DNS-as-exfil-channel; (f) no alarm set; (g) no live-proof demo for the client's security team. Each of these is a candidate discriminating assertion.

suggestions.assertion: Explicitly warns that a SaaS observability vendor (e.g. hosted Langfuse/Datadog) breaks the residency clause
suggestions.reason: Both runs pass, but they differ in strength: the baseline offers 'redact payloads at the SDK boundary and ship only spans + metrics' as an acceptable alternative to moving the trace store, while the with_skill run rules SaaS observability out entirely ('No SaaS observability ... no vendor-side OTLP collector'). If the skill's position is that redaction-to-a-vendor is NOT an acceptable residency answer, the assertion should say so — as written it accepts both.

The baseline invented a statistic ('~90% of enterprises') that no assertion penalizes. Consider a negative assertion class (e.g. 'makes no unsourced quantitative claims about client behavior') if fabricated precision matters for this skill's credibility in front of security reviewers.

eval_feedback.overall: Baseline and with_skill both 7/7. The assertions measure the well-known half of the problem (what moves / what stays) and none measure the default-state, evidence, and enforcement half where the skill actually adds value. Recommend rewriting 2-3 assertions toward off-by-default enablement, log immutability, and the Global-inference residency trap.
